summary.text: Agamemnon's aristeia broke against Hector's charge; Diomedes and Odysseus fell wounded, and Paris' arrow sent the healer Machaon to the ships in Nestor's chariot — until, at the Achaean wall, Hector smashed a gate with a boulder and the Trojans poured through.

chapters.title: Agamemnon's day
chapters.text: Dawn brought Agamemnon's aristeia: the son of Atreus drove the Trojans across the plain to the Scaean gates, his invincible hands spattered with gore. Zeus sent Iris to Hector with a warning — hold back while Agamemnon raged, and when he was wounded, then Hector might drive the host. Coön's spear pierced the king's arm below the elbow; he fought on until the pain came, then left the field in his chariot, and the tide turned.

chapters.title: Diomedes and Odysseus down
chapters.text: Diomedes fought on until Paris' arrow struck his foot; he climbed into his chariot and withdrew. Odysseus stood alone among the Trojans until Socus' spear tore his side; at his cry Menelaus and Ajax ran to him, and while Ajax held the Trojans off behind his tower-like shield, Menelaus led him out by the hand to his chariot. The nested episode on the Night Raid tells Book 10, the night before, when Odysseus and Diomedes struck in the darkness; here the daylight fighting leaves the host's best men wounded.

chapters.title: Machaon and the healers
chapters.text: Paris' arrow struck Machaon the healer in the right shoulder, and at Idomeneus' urging Nestor took him into his chariot and drove to the ships — for a healer is worth many other men. Paris shot Eurypylus too, in the thigh, and he limped back from the fighting. Achilles, watching from his ship, saw Nestor's chariot pass and sent Patroclus to learn who was hurt; the first step toward the armour Patroclus would borrow.

chapters.title: Ajax on the wall
chapters.text: Book 12 opens with a glance ahead: once Troy had fallen, Poseidon and Apollo would turn the rivers of the Troad against the Achaeans' wall and wash it away. Now the Trojans assaulted it — Hector and Polydamas at the ditch, Sarpedon and Glaucus leading the Lycians against Menestheus' tower, where Ajax crushed Epicles with a stone and Teucer's arrow drove Glaucus from the wall. Then Hector, calling on the Trojans to fire the ships, lifted a boulder two strong men could scarcely have raised, smashed the gate, and the Trojans poured over the wall and through it as the Achaeans fled among the ships.
